pos: v. (to explain the meaning; rendering Hebrew pathar, Greek diermeneuo)
etymology: From Latin interpretari, to explain. Scripture consistently treats interpretation as a gift given rather than a skill mastered.
biblical_def: To interpret is to explain a meaning. Joseph refuses credit for it: “Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you” (Gen 40:8). Daniel says the same before Nebuchadnezzar — there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets (Dan 2:28). Paul regulates tongues by it: “if there be no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church” (1Co 14:28), and Peter states the rule for prophecy: “no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation” (2Pe 1:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines interpret as to explain the meaning of words to a person who does not understand them; to expound; to translate into intelligible or familiar language.
webster_full: INTERPRET, v.t. To explain the meaning of words to a person who does not understand them; to expound; to translate unintelligible words into intelligible ones.
2. To explain or unfold the meaning of predictions, prophecies, or any thing not understood.
3. To decipher.
scriptures: Gen 40:8
And they said unto him, We have dreamed a dream, and there is no interpreter of it. And Joseph said unto them, Do not interpretations belong to God? tell me them, I pray you.
Knowing this first, that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
But if there be no interpreter, let him keep silence in the church; and let him speak to himself, and to God.
Dan 2:28
But there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days. Thy dream, and the visions of thy head upon thy bed, are these;
corruption_summary: Interpretation is treated as a private right, and Peter's rule is that no scripture is of any private interpretation — the text belongs to the church, not to the reader alone.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Peter 1:20-21 gives the reason for the rule: no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation. For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man. The logic runs from origin to method — because Scripture was not privately produced, it is not privately interpreted. A reading that no other believer, no confession, and no century has ever arrived at is not thereby original; it is unmoored.

Joseph and Daniel both hold power over a king by the same gift and both refuse to hold it. Do not interpretations belong to God? and It is not in me: God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace. Each had every incentive to accept credit, and each deflected it before explaining anything. That is the posture of anyone handling a text he did not write.
roots_summary: Hebrew pathar (H6622), to interpret a dream; Greek diermeneuo (G1329), to explain thoroughly; epilusis (G1955), a loosing or interpretation.
roots_lines: Hebrew pathar (H6622) — to interpret; Genesis 40:8, 16, 41:12.
Greek diermeneuo (G1329) — to interpret; Luke 24:27, 1 Corinthians 12:30, 14:5.
Greek epilusis (G1955) — interpretation, unloosing; only 2 Peter 1:20.
usage: “Do not interpretations belong to God?” — credit deflected before explanation.
“No prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation” — the origin sets the method.
“If there be no interpreter, let him keep silence” — unexplained speech serves nobody.

pos: v. (to compare; rendering Hebrew damah, Greek homoioo)
etymology: From like. To liken is to set two things side by side — and Isaiah's question is whether anything may be set beside God.
biblical_def: To liken is to compare. Isaiah asks the question idolatry cannot answer: “To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?” (Isa 40:18), and again, “To whom will ye liken me, and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be like?” (Isa 46:5). Christ likens freely in the other direction: “Whereunto shall I liken the kingdom of God?” (Luk 13:20), and ends the Sermon on the Mount by likening two builders (Mat 7:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines liken as to compare; to represent as resembling or similar.
webster_full: LIKEN, v.t. To compare; to represent as resembling or similar.
LIKENESS, n. Resemblance in form; similitude.
2. Resemblance; form; external appearance.
scriptures: To whom then will ye liken God? or what likeness will ye compare unto him?
Isa 46:5
To whom will ye liken me, and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be like?
And again he said, Whereunto shall I liken the kingdom of God?
Mat 7:24
Therefore whosoever heareth these sayings of mine, and doeth them, I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock:
corruption_summary: God is described by whatever comparison feels warm, and Isaiah's question rules out the whole method — there is nothing to set beside Him.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 40:18 is asked in the middle of the chapter that measures the waters in the hollow of a hand and weighs the mountains in scales: to whom then will ye liken God? The answer expected is silence. What follows is a description of a craftsman making an idol and fastening it so it will not topple — the only likeness available is one a man builds and then has to steady. Every image of God we construct requires our support.

Christ's likening runs the opposite direction and is therefore safe. He does not compare God to something greater but explains the kingdom by things smaller — a seed, a treasure, a net, a man building on rock. The Creator may condescend to a comparison; the creature may not manufacture one. That asymmetry is why the parables are revelation and idols are not.
roots_summary: Hebrew damah (H1819), to be like, compare; demuth (H1823), likeness; Greek homoioo (G3666), to make like.
roots_lines: Hebrew damah (H1819) — to liken, compare; Isaiah 40:18, 25, 46:5.
Hebrew demuth (H1823) — likeness; Genesis 1:26, in our image, after our likeness.
Greek homoioo (G3666) — to liken; Matthew 7:24, 11:16, Luke 13:18-20.
usage: “To whom then will ye liken God?” — the question expecting silence.
“Whereunto shall I liken the kingdom of God?” — the Creator may condescend to compare.
“I will liken him unto a wise man, which built his house upon a rock” — the sermon's last image.

pos: v. (valued, reckoned; rendering Hebrew chashab, Greek hegeomai)
etymology: From Latin aestimare, to appraise. Esteem is a valuation, and Scripture repeatedly records valuations that were exactly wrong.
biblical_def: To be esteemed is to be valued. Isaiah records the crowd's appraisal of the Servant: “he is despised and rejected of men… and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not” (Isa 53:3). Christ states the general rule: “that which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God” (Luk 16:15). Job esteemed God's words more than his necessary food (Job 23:12), and Paul counted all things loss (Php 3:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines esteem as to set a value on, whether high or low; to estimate; to value; and to prize, to regard with reverence, respect or friendship.
webster_full: ESTEEM, v.t. To set a value on, whether high or low; to estimate; to value.
2. To prize; to set a high value on; to regard with reverence, respect or friendship.
3. To hold in opinion; to repute; to think.
scriptures: Isa 53:3
He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were our faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not.
And he said unto them, Ye are they which justify yourselves before men; but God knoweth your hearts: for that which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God.
Neither have I gone back from the commandment of his lips; I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food.
Php 3:8

Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
corruption_summary: Public esteem is treated as a rough measure of worth, and Christ says the correlation runs backwards where God is the appraiser.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 16:15 is spoken to Pharisees who derided Him over money: ye are they which justify yourselves before men; but God knoweth your hearts: for that which is highly esteemed among men is abomination in the sight of God. The sentence is not that popularity is suspect but that the two scales run opposite. That does not make obscurity a virtue — it makes public valuation useless as evidence either way.

Isaiah 53:3 records the misappraisal that matters most: we esteemed him not. The verse is a confession in the first person plural. It was not merely that the world got it wrong; the speakers include themselves. Any honest reading of that chapter has to admit that had we been standing there, our valuation would have been the same one.
roots_summary: Hebrew chashab (H2803), to reckon, esteem; Greek hegeomai (G2233), to consider, count; hupselos (G5308), high — highly esteemed in Luke 16:15.
roots_lines: Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to reckon, esteem, impute; Isaiah 53:3-4.
Greek hegeomai (G2233) — to count, esteem; Philippians 2:3, 3:8, 1 Thessalonians 5:13.
Greek bdelugma (G946) — abomination; Luke 16:15.
usage: “He was despised, and we esteemed him not” — a first-person confession.
“Highly esteemed among men is abomination… before God” — two scales, opposite readings.
“I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food” — Job's appraisal.

pos: adj. (well-pleasing, received with favour; rendering Hebrew ratson, Greek euarestos)
etymology: From Latin acceptare, to receive willingly. Acceptability in Scripture is never assumed; it is determined by the One receiving.
biblical_def: Acceptable means received with favour. Christ reads Isaiah in Nazareth and stops mid-sentence at “the acceptable year of the LORD” (Luk 4:19). Paul urges bodies presented as “a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God” (Rom 12:1) and describes the Philippians' gift as “an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God” (Php 4:18). The psalmist prays that the words of his mouth and the meditation of his heart be acceptable (Psa 19:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines acceptable as that may be received with pleasure; pleasing to a receiver; gratifying; agreeable; welcome.
webster_full: ACCEPTABLE, a. That may be received with pleasure; hence pleasing to a receiver; gratifying; agreeable; welcome.
scriptures: Rom 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
Luk 4:19
To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.
Php 4:18
But I have all, and abound: I am full, having received of Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God.
Let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer.
corruption_summary: Worship is evaluated by whether the worshipper found it meaningful, and Scripture evaluates it by whether God found it acceptable.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 19:14 makes the standard external: let the words of my mouth, and the meditation of my heart, be acceptable in thy sight, O LORD, my strength, and my redeemer. Both the public and the private — mouth and meditation — are submitted for approval to a Judge outside the worshipper. The prayer assumes the possibility of unacceptable worship offered sincerely, which is the possibility Cain discovered.

Luke 4:19 is remarkable for where Christ stopped. He read Isaiah 61 through to preach the acceptable year of the Lord, closed the book, and sat down — leaving unread the next clause, and the day of vengeance of our God. Between the acceptable year and the day of vengeance falls the whole present age. He announced the half that had arrived.
roots_summary: Hebrew ratson (H7522), favour, acceptance, will; Greek euarestos (G2101), well-pleasing; dektos (G1184), acceptable.
roots_lines: Hebrew ratson (H7522) — favour, acceptance; Psalm 19:14, Isaiah 61:2, the acceptable year.
Greek euarestos (G2101) — well-pleasing; Romans 12:1-2, Philippians 4:18, Hebrews 13:21.
Greek dektos (G1184) — acceptable; Luke 4:19, 24, Acts 10:35.
usage: “A living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God” — the standard is His reception.
“The acceptable year of the LORD” — and He stopped before the day of vengeance.
“Let the words of my mouth… be acceptable in thy sight” — mouth and meditation submitted.

pos: adj. (enough for the need; rendering Greek hikanos and arkeo)
etymology: From Latin sufficere, to be enough. Sufficiency in Scripture is measured against a demand, and Paul's answer locates it outside himself.
biblical_def: Sufficient means enough. Paul asks the ministry's hardest question and answers it twice: “who is sufficient for these things?” (2Co 2:16), and later, “not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God” (2Co 3:5). Christ's word to him in weakness is the same: “My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2Co 12:9). And each day carries its own load: “sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof” (Mat 6:34).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sufficient as enough; equal to the end proposed; adequate to wants; competent; qualified.
webster_full: SUFFICIENT, a. Enough; equal to the end proposed; adequate to wants; competent.
2. Qualified; competent; possessing adequate talents or accomplishments.
3. Fit; able; of competent power or ability.
scriptures: To the one we are the savour of death unto death; and to the other the savour of life unto life. And who is sufficient for these things?
Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God;

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Mat 6:34
Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
corruption_summary: Adequacy is pursued through training and capacity, and Paul's answer to who is sufficient? is that nobody is, and that the sufficiency is supplied.
corruption_paragraphs: 2 Corinthians 2:16 asks the question every honest minister eventually asks: who is sufficient for these things? Paul lets it stand unanswered for a chapter before returning to it: not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God. Not merely to do — to think. The inadequacy runs down to the level of forming a thought, and the supply runs from God rather than from preparation.

Matthew 6:34 applies the same word to anxiety with unexpected gentleness: sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof. Christ does not deny that each day carries trouble; He states it plainly and confines it. Tomorrow's difficulty added to today's makes a load no grace was issued for, because grace is issued daily. Borrowing trouble is therefore not merely unwise but outside the supply.
roots_summary: Greek hikanos (G2425), sufficient, competent; arkeo (G714), to be enough — my grace is sufficient; hikanotes (G2426), sufficiency.
roots_lines: Greek hikanos (G2425) — sufficient, worthy; 2 Corinthians 2:16, 3:5, Matthew 8:8, I am not worthy.
Greek arkeo (G714) — to suffice; 2 Corinthians 12:9, Hebrews 13:5, be content with such things as ye have.
Greek autarkeia (G841) — contentment, sufficiency; 2 Corinthians 9:8, 1 Timothy 6:6.
usage: “Who is sufficient for these things?” — left unanswered for a chapter.
“Our sufficiency is of God” — the inadequacy reaches down to thinking.
“My grace is sufficient for thee” — enough, and no more than enough.

pos: v. (dried up, shrunken; rendering Hebrew yabesh, Greek xeraino)
etymology: From wither, a variant of weather — to be worn by exposure. Scripture uses it of hands, plants, and hearts.
biblical_def: Withered means dried up. Christ heals a man with a withered hand on the sabbath and asks, “Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill?” (Mar 3:4). The stony-ground seed springs up and withers for lack of root (Mat 13:6). Jonah's gourd withers overnight (Jon 4:7), and the psalmist confesses, “My heart is smitten, and withered like grass” (Psa 102:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wither as to fade; to lose its natural freshness; to become sapless; to dry; and to waste, to pine away.
webster_full: WITHER, v.i. To fade; to lose its natural freshness; to become sapless; to dry.
2. To waste; to pine away; as animal bodies.
3. To lose or want animal moisture.
scriptures: Mar 3:4
And he saith unto them, Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill? But they held their peace.
Mat 13:6
And when the sun was up, they were scorched; and because they had no root, they withered away.
Jon 4:7
But God prepared a worm when the morning rose the next day, and it smote the gourd that it withered.
My heart is smitten, and withered like grass; so that I forget to eat my bread.
corruption_summary: Doing good is postponed for the sake of keeping a rule, and Christ framed the sabbath question as save life or kill — leaving no neutral third option.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 3:4 removes the middle ground: is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill? The Pharisees had assumed a third category — do nothing, and remain safe. Christ denies it. Withholding available good is not neutrality; and the text notes He looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, which is the only recorded instance of His anger in that Gospel.

Psalm 102:4 gives the word its inward use: my heart is smitten, and withered like grass; so that I forget to eat my bread. The psalm is titled a prayer of the afflicted when he is overwhelmed. Withering is not always a moral failure; sometimes it is simply what grief does to a person, and Scripture supplies the vocabulary rather than a rebuke.
roots_summary: Hebrew yabesh (H3001), to dry up, wither; Greek xeraino (G3583), to dry; xeros (G3584), dry — the withered hand.
roots_lines: Hebrew yabesh (H3001) — to dry up, wither; Jonah 4:7, Psalm 102:11, Isaiah 40:7.
Greek xeros (G3584) — dry, withered; Mark 3:1-3, Luke 6:6.
Greek xeraino (G3583) — to wither; Matthew 13:6, 21:19, Mark 11:21.
usage: “Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days?” — no neutral third option.
“Because they had no root, they withered away” — the stony ground.
“My heart is smitten, and withered like grass” — grief given words.

pos: n. (the base left after felling; rendering Hebrew iqqar)
etymology: Middle English stumpe. A stump is what remains when a tree is cut — in Scripture, sometimes a ruin and sometimes a reservation.
biblical_def: A stump is the base left after felling. Nebuchadnezzar's dream tree is cut down but the stump is preserved: “leave the stump of his roots in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass… till seven times pass over him” (Dan 4:15) — and the interpretation is that his kingdom shall be sure to him after he has known that the heavens do rule (Dan 4:26). The stump of Dagon is the opposite case: only the stump of the idol was left to him (1Sa 5:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stump as the stub of a tree, plant or vegetable, that part of the stem which remains fixed in the earth when the stem is cut down.
webster_full: STUMP, n. The stub of a tree, plant or vegetable; that part of the stem which remains fixed in the earth when the stem is cut down; as the stump of an oak.
2. The part of a limb of the body remaining after amputation.
scriptures: Dan 4:15

Nevertheless leave the stump of his roots in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth:
Dan 4:26
And whereas they commanded to leave the stump of the tree roots; thy kingdom shall be sure unto thee, after that thou shalt have known that the heavens do rule.

And when they arose early on the morrow morning, behold, Dagon was fallen upon his face to the ground before the ark of the LORD; and the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands were cut off upon the threshold; only the stump of Dagon was left to him. the
Isa 6:13

But yet in it shall be a tenth, and it shall return, and shall be eaten: as a teil tree, and as an oak, whose substance is in them, when they cast their leaves: so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof.
corruption_summary: Discipline is read as destruction, and Daniel's dream carefully preserves a stump because the humbling had an appointed end.
corruption_paragraphs: Daniel 4:15 contains the mercy inside the sentence: leave the stump of his roots in the earth. The tree is cut, the branches lopped, the leaves shaken off, and the beasts driven out — but the root is banded with iron and brass and kept. The interpretation makes the point explicit: thy kingdom shall be sure unto thee, after that thou shalt have known that the heavens do rule. The stump was the promise of restoration, banded so nothing could remove it.

Dagon's stump is the counter-case. The image fell before the ark twice; the second time the head and both palms were cut off upon the threshold, and only the stump of Dagon was left to him. A god that has to be set back in place by its worshippers, and finally cannot be, is what remains when the true God enters the room.
roots_summary: Aramaic iqqar (H6136), a stump or root-stock; Hebrew Dagon retains only its trunk in 1 Samuel 5:4; matstsebeth (H4678), a stump or pillar, in Isaiah 6:13.
roots_lines: Aramaic iqqar (H6136) — stump, root; Daniel 4:15, 23, 26.
Hebrew matstsebeth (H4678) — substance, stump; Isaiah 6:13, so the holy seed shall be the substance thereof.
Hebrew geza (H1503) — stem, stock; Isaiah 11:1, a rod out of the stem of Jesse.
usage: “Leave the stump of his roots in the earth” — mercy inside the sentence.
“After that thou shalt have known that the heavens do rule” — the humbling had an end.
“Only the stump of Dagon was left” — the idol that could not be propped up again.

pos: v. (covered over, submerged; rendering Hebrew ataph and kasah)
etymology: Over with whelm, to turn upside down over something. To be overwhelmed is to be buried under, not merely troubled.
biblical_def: To be overwhelmed is to be covered over. David prays from it: “when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I” (Psa 61:2). Psalm 142's title says he was in the cave, and the psalm records, “when my spirit was overwhelmed within me, then thou knewest my path” (Psa 142:3). Psalm 102 is titled a prayer of the afflicted “when he is overwhelmed, and poureth out his complaint before the LORD”.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines overwhelm as to overspread or crush beneath something violent and weighty; to immerse and bear down; and to overlook gloomily.
webster_full: OVERWHELM, v.t. To overspread or crush beneath something violent and weighty, that covers or encompasses the whole; as, to overwhelm with waves.
2. To immerse and bear down; in a figurative sense; as, to be overwhelmed with cares, afflictions or business.
scriptures: Psa 61:2
From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I.
When my spirit was overwhelmed within me, then thou knewest my path. In the way wherein I walked have they privily laid a snare for me.
Psa 77:3
I remembered God, and was troubled: I complained, and my spirit was overwhelmed. Selah.
Therefore is my spirit overwhelmed within me; my heart within me is desolate.
corruption_summary: Being overwhelmed is treated as a failure of faith, and three of David's psalms use the word about himself while still addressing God.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 61:2 does not ask for the feeling to stop: from the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I. He asks for relocation rather than relief. The rock is higher than he is — a place he cannot reach unaided, which is why the request is lead me. Overwhelmed prayer in Scripture keeps its grammar even when it loses its footing.

Psalm 142:3 supplies the sentence worth memorizing for such seasons: when my spirit was overwhelmed within me, then thou knewest my path. Two clauses, and the second answers the first without denying it. He does not say the overwhelming was imagined or that his path became clear. He says Someone else knew it while he could not see it.
roots_summary: Hebrew ataph (H5848), to be feeble, faint, overwhelmed; kasah (H3680), to cover; shataph (H7857), to overflow.
roots_lines: Hebrew ataph (H5848) — to faint, be overwhelmed; Psalm 61:2, 102 title, 142:3, 143:4.
Hebrew kasah (H3680) — to cover; Psalm 55:5, horror hath overwhelmed me.
Hebrew tsur (H6697) — rock; Psalm 61:2, the rock that is higher than I.
usage: “Lead me to the rock that is higher than I” — relocation, not relief.
“When my spirit was overwhelmed… then thou knewest my path” — the second clause answers the first.
“When he is overwhelmed, and poureth out his complaint” — a psalm titled for this.

pos: adj., v. (lame; to waver; rendering Hebrew pasach, Greek cholos)
etymology: Old English healt, lame. The same verb means to limp and to hesitate — which is exactly Elijah's point on Carmel.
biblical_def: Halt means lame, and also to waver. Elijah uses both senses in one challenge: “How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him” (1Ki 18:21) — the same Hebrew verb describes Baal's prophets leaping about their altar. Christ commands that the halt be brought in to the great supper (Luk 14:21), and Jacob halted upon his thigh after Peniel (Gen 32:31).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines halt as to limp, to be lame; to hesitate, to stand in doubt whether to proceed or what to do; and as an adjective, lame, limping.
webster_full: HALT, v.i. To stop in walking; to hold.
2. To limp; that is, to stop with lameness.
3. To hesitate; to stand in doubt whether to proceed, or what to do.
HALT, a. Lame; that limps.
scriptures: And Elijah came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him. And the people answered him not a word.

So that servant came, and shewed his lord these things. Then the master of the house being angry said to his servant, Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind.
And as he passed over Penuel the sun rose upon him, and he halted upon his thigh.
Joh 5:3
In these lay a great multitude of impotent folk, of blind, halt, withered, waiting for the moving of the water.
corruption_summary: Undecided allegiance is described as open-mindedness, and Elijah calls it limping — a gait, not a position.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Kings 18:21 is a pun with teeth. The verb rendered halt means to limp, and Elijah applies it to a nation trying to walk on two legs of unequal length: how long halt ye between two opinions? Verse 26 uses the same word of Baal's prophets leaping upon the altar. Israel's indecision and the pagans' frenzy are described by one verb. And the people's response is recorded in four words: and the people answered him not a word.

Luke 14:21 puts the literal sense to gracious use. When the invited guests excuse themselves, the master sends his servant into the streets and lanes to bring in the poor, and the maimed, and the halt, and the blind. The banquet is filled with people who could not have walked there quickly, and the house is filled precisely because the confident declined.
roots_summary: Hebrew pasach (H6452), to limp, to pass over — the same root as Passover; Greek cholos (G5560), lame.
roots_lines: Hebrew pasach (H6452) — to limp, hesitate, pass over; 1 Kings 18:21, 26, Exodus 12:13.
Greek cholos (G5560) — lame, halt; Luke 14:21, Matthew 18:8, John 5:3.
Hebrew tsala (H6760) — to limp; Genesis 32:31, Micah 4:6, I will assemble her that halteth.
usage: “How long halt ye between two opinions?” — indecision described as a limp.
“The people answered him not a word” — the reply to the question.
“Bring in hither the poor, and the maimed, and the halt” — the house filled by the slow.

pos: v. (regarded with compassion; rendering Hebrew chamal and racham)
etymology: From Latin pietas, dutiful feeling. Pity in Scripture is active compassion — the word for a father's feeling toward his children.
biblical_def: To be pitied is to be regarded with compassion. The psalmist uses it of God: “Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him. For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust” (Psa 103:13–14). Ezekiel describes an abandoned infant that “none eye pitied thee” until God passed by (Eze 16:5–6). Job protests to his friends, “Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends” (Job 19:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines pity as the feeling or suffering of one person, excited by the distresses of another; sympathy with the grief or misery of another; compassion or fellow-suffering.
webster_full: PITY, n. The feeling or suffering of one person, excited by the distresses of another; sympathy with the grief or misery of another; compassion or fellow-suffering.
PITY, v.t. To feel pain or grief for one in distress; to compassionate; to have sympathy for.
scriptures: Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him.
For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust.
Eze 16:5
None eye pitied thee, to do any of these unto thee, to have compassion upon thee; but thou wast cast out in the open field, to the lothing of thy person, in the day that thou wast born.
Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me.
corruption_summary: Pity is resented as condescension, and Psalm 103 makes it the tenderest thing said about God's dealing with weak people.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 103:13-14 gives the reason with the image: like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him. For he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust. God's compassion is grounded in accurate knowledge of the material He is dealing with. He is not disappointed by our frailty because He is not surprised by it — He formed the dust in the first place, and He remembers.

Ezekiel 16:5-6 is the most graphic picture of unpitied helplessness in Scripture: none eye pitied thee… but thou wast cast out in the open field, to the lothing of thy person. And when I passed by thee, and saw thee polluted in thine own blood, I said unto thee… Live. The nation's whole existence is traced to a moment when God pitied what everyone else had walked past.
roots_summary: Hebrew chamal (H2550), to spare, have compassion; racham (H7355), to love deeply, as a womb — the root of tender mercies.
roots_lines: Hebrew racham (H7355) — to have compassion, pity; Psalm 103:13, Isaiah 49:15.
Hebrew chamal (H2550) — to spare, pity; Ezekiel 16:5, Exodus 2:6, of Pharaoh's daughter.
Hebrew yetser (H3336) — frame, form; Psalm 103:14, he knoweth our frame.
usage: “Like as a father pitieth his children” — compassion grounded in accurate knowledge.
“He remembereth that we are dust” — not surprised by frailty.
“None eye pitied thee… I said unto thee… Live” — the moment a nation began.

pos: v. (corrected by discipline; rendering Hebrew yasar, Greek paideuo)
etymology: From Latin castigare, to make pure. Chastisement is corrective rather than penal — the Greek word is built on the word for a child.
biblical_def: To be chastised is to be corrected. Rehoboam's advisers give the word its cruel political use: “my father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions” (1Ki 12:11). Jeremiah's Ephraim prays, “Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised, as a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke: turn thou me, and I shall be turned” (Jer 31:18). Isaiah says of the Servant, “the chastisement of our peace was upon him” (Isa 53:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines chastise as to correct by punishment; to punish; to inflict pain for the purpose of reclaiming an offender; and to reduce to order or obedience.
webster_full: CHASTISE, v.t. To correct by punishment; to punish; to inflict pain by stripes, or in other manner, for the purpose of punishing an offender and recalling him to his duty.
2. To reduce to order or obedience; to restrain; to awe; to correct.
3. To purify from errors or faults.
scriptures: I have surely heard Ephraim bemoaning himself thus; Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised, as a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke: turn thou me, and I shall be turned; for thou art the LORD my God.
Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
And now whereas my father did lade you with a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke: my father hath chastised you with whips, but I will chastise you with scorpions.
Heb 12:6
For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.
corruption_summary: Chastening is confused with punishment, and Hebrews grounds it in sonship — whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth, and scourgeth every son whom he receiveth.
corruption_paragraphs: Jeremiah 31:18 is a model prayer for anyone under discipline. Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised, as a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke: turn thou me, and I shall be turned; for thou art the LORD my God. He admits the chastening, admits his own untrained resistance, and then asks God to do the turning rather than promising to turn himself. The next verse adds, surely after that I was turned, I repented.

Isaiah 53:5 makes the crucial distinction the doctrine depends on: the chastisement of our peace was upon him. The penal stroke fell on the Servant, which is why what falls on a believer afterward is corrective rather than condemnatory. Hebrews 12 draws the conclusion — if ye endure chastening, God dealeth with you as with sons — and adds the uncomfortable inverse about those who receive none.
roots_summary: Hebrew yasar (H3256), to discipline, instruct; musar (H4148), correction, instruction; Greek paideuo (G3811), to train a child.
roots_lines: Hebrew yasar (H3256) — to chasten, instruct; Jeremiah 31:18, Proverbs 19:18, Deuteronomy 8:5.
Hebrew musar (H4148) — chastisement, instruction; Isaiah 53:5, Proverbs 3:11.
Greek paideuo (G3811) — to instruct, chasten; Hebrews 12:6-10, Revelation 3:19.
usage: “Turn thou me, and I shall be turned” — asking God to do the turning.
“The chastisement of our peace was upon him” — the penal stroke fell elsewhere.
“As a bullock unaccustomed to the yoke” — honest about the resistance.

pos: v. (led astray; rendering Hebrew taah, Greek planao)
etymology: From Latin seducere, to lead aside. Seduction is a leading, which means it requires a guide and a road.
biblical_def: To be seduced is to be led astray. Isaiah charges leaders with it: “they that lead thee cause thee to err” (Isa 9:16), and Ezekiel condemns prophets that “have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace” (Eze 13:10). John writes, “these things have I written unto you concerning them that seduce you” (1Jn 2:26), and Paul warns of “seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils” in the latter times (1Ti 4:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines seduce as to draw aside or entice from the path of rectitude and duty in any manner, by flattery, promises, bribes or otherwise; to tempt and lead to iniquity; to corrupt.
webster_full: SEDUCE, v.t. To draw aside or entice from the path of rectitude and duty in any manner, by flattery, promises, bribes or otherwise; to tempt and lead to iniquity; to corrupt; to deprave.
SEDUCER, n. One who seduces; one who by temptation or arts, entices another to depart from the path of rectitude and duty.
scriptures: Because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace; and one built up a wall, and, lo, others daubed it with untempered morter:
These things have I written unto you concerning them that seduce you.
Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils;
Isa 9:16
For the leaders of this people cause them to err; and they that are led of them are destroyed.
corruption_summary: False comfort is mistaken for pastoral kindness, and Ezekiel's charge against the seducing prophets is one sentence: they said Peace, and there was no peace.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 13:10 identifies the mechanism of seduction as reassurance rather than temptation: because, even because they have seduced my people, saying, Peace; and there was no peace. The image that follows is builders daubing a flimsy wall with untempered morter — making a dangerous structure look finished. Nobody was told to sin; they were told everything was fine. That is a gentler-sounding and more effective way to destroy a congregation.

1 John 2:26-27 pairs the warning with a remedy that does not depend on expertise: these things have I written unto you concerning them that seduce you. But the anointing which ye have received of him abideth in you. Ordinary believers are given an internal witness sufficient to detect a lie, which is why John writes to the whole church rather than to its leaders about this danger.
roots_summary: Hebrew taah (H8582), to wander, cause to err; Greek planao (G4105), to lead astray; planos (G4108), a deceiver.
roots_lines: Hebrew taah (H8582) — to wander, seduce; Ezekiel 13:10, Isaiah 9:16, 2 Kings 21:9.
Greek planao (G4105) — to lead astray; 1 John 2:26, Revelation 2:20, 12:9.
Greek planos (G4108) — seducing, deceiving; 1 Timothy 4:1, seducing spirits.
usage: “Saying, Peace; and there was no peace” — seduction by reassurance.
“Daubed it with untempered morter” — a flimsy wall made to look finished.
“The anointing which ye have received… abideth in you” — the remedy given to all.

pos: v. (deprived by deceit; rendering Hebrew ashaq, Greek apostereo)
etymology: From Latin defraudare, to cheat. Fraud is theft conducted through a transaction rather than against one.
biblical_def: To defraud is to deprive by deceit. Samuel's public audit invites the charge and is cleared of it: “Whose ox have I taken? or whose ass have I taken? or whom have I defrauded?… And they said, Thou hast not defrauded us” (1Sa 12:3–4). Paul asks the Corinthians, “why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?” (1Co 6:7), and warns that no man “go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter” (1Th 4:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines defraud as to deprive of right, either by obtaining something by deception or artifice, or by taking something wrongfully without the knowledge or consent of the owner; to cheat; to cozen.
webster_full: DEFRAUD, v.t. To deprive of right, either by obtaining something by deception or artifice, or by taking something wrongfully without the knowledge or consent of the owner; to cheat; to cozen.
2. To withhold wrongfully from another what is due to him.
scriptures: Behold, here I am: witness against me before the LORD, and before his anointed: whose ox have I taken? or whose ass have I taken? or whom have I defrauded? whom have I oppressed? or of whose hand have I received any bribe to blind mine eyes therewith? and I will restore it you.
And they said, Thou hast not defrauded us, nor oppressed us, neither hast thou taken ought of any man's hand.
Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?
That no man go beyond and defraud his brother in any matter: because that the Lord is the avenger of all such, as we also have forewarned you and testified.
corruption_summary: Christians take one another to court to recover losses, and Paul asks why they do not simply accept being defrauded rather than testify against the gospel.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Corinthians 6:7 asks a question that has never been comfortable: now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded? Paul does not say the plaintiffs were wrong about the facts. He says winning a public case against a brother is itself a defeat, because the watching world learns what the church actually believes about property.

Samuel's audit in 1 Samuel 12 is the model for anyone in office. He stands before the whole nation at the end of a lifetime and asks them to name any ox, any ass, any bribe, any oppression — and calls the LORD and the king as witnesses to their answer. Voluntary, public, specific accountability offered by a man nobody was investigating.
roots_summary: Hebrew ashaq (H6231), to oppress, defraud; ratsats (H7533), to crush; Greek apostereo (G650), to defraud, keep back.
roots_lines: Hebrew ashaq (H6231) — to oppress, defraud; 1 Samuel 12:3-4, Leviticus 19:13.
Greek apostereo (G650) — to defraud, deprive; 1 Corinthians 6:7-8, 1 Timothy 6:5, James 5:4.
Greek pleonekteo (G4122) — to overreach, defraud; 1 Thessalonians 4:6, 2 Corinthians 7:2.
usage: “Whom have I defrauded?” — an audit nobody demanded.
“Why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded?” — winning as a form of losing.
“That no man go beyond and defraud his brother” — the boundary in business.

pos: v. (grudged another's good; rendering Hebrew qana, Greek zeloo)
etymology: From Latin invidere, to look upon with malice — literally to look against. Envy is a way of seeing before it is a way of acting.
biblical_def: To envy is to grudge another's good. Genesis notes it at each fracture: Isaac's wells — “the Philistines envied him” (Gen 26:14); Rachel envying Leah (Gen 30:1); and Joseph's brothers — “his brethren envied him; but his father observed the saying” (Gen 37:11). Peter names the motive behind the crucifixion: Pilate “knew that for envy they had delivered him” (Mat 27:18). Proverbs says, “envy the rottenness of the bones” (Pro 14:30).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines envy as pain, uneasiness, mortification or discontent excited by the sight of another's superiority or success, accompanied with some degree of hatred or malignity.
webster_full: ENVY, n. Pain, uneasiness, mortification or discontent excited by the sight of another's superiority or success, accompanied with some degree of hatred or malignity, and often with a desire or an effort to depreciate the person.
ENVY, v.t. To feel uneasiness, mortification or discontent, at the sight of superior excellence, reputation or happiness enjoyed by another.
scriptures: And his brethren envied him; but his father observed the saying.
For he knew that for envy they had delivered him.
A sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones.
For he had possession of flocks, and possession of herds, and great store of servants: and the Philistines envied him.
corruption_summary: Envy is the one deadly sin nobody boasts of and everybody practises, and Proverbs locates its damage in the envier's own bones.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 14:30 sets the diagnosis physically: a sound heart is the life of the flesh: but envy the rottenness of the bones. The harm named is internal and structural. Envy does nothing to the person envied; it decays the frame of the one carrying it, slowly and out of sight, which is why it can be maintained for decades without anyone noticing including its host.

Matthew 27:18 records the coldest observation in the passion narrative: for he knew that for envy they had delivered him. A Roman governor, no theologian, correctly diagnosed the motive of the religious leadership at a glance. Envy had brought the chief priests to the point of engineering a judicial murder, and an outsider could see it. That is what the sin is capable of when it is given institutional power.
roots_summary: Hebrew qana (H7065), to be zealous or envious — the same verb for holy jealousy; Greek phthonos (G5355), envy; zeloo (G2206), to be zealous or envious.
roots_lines: Hebrew qana (H7065) — to envy, be jealous; Genesis 26:14, 30:1, 37:11, Psalm 73:3.
Greek phthonos (G5355) — envy; Matthew 27:18, Romans 1:29, Galatians 5:21, Philippians 1:15.
Greek zeloo (G2206) — to be zealous, envy; Acts 7:9, the patriarchs, moved with envy, sold Joseph.
usage: “His brethren envied him” — the fracture that sold a brother.
“He knew that for envy they had delivered him” — diagnosed by a pagan governor.
“Envy the rottenness of the bones” — the damage is to the envier.

pos: n., adj. (the earliest ripe fruit; rendering Hebrew bikkurah)
etymology: First with ripe. The firstripe fig is the earliest of the crop — prized, eaten immediately, and gone before the harvest proper.
biblical_def: Firstripe describes the earliest ripe fruit. Micah uses it for a rare and vanished thing: “Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits… there is no cluster to eat: my soul desired the firstripe fruit” (Mic 7:1). Hosea uses it of God's first delight in Israel: “I saw your fathers as the firstripe in the fig tree at her first time” (Hos 9:10). The law commands the firstripe grapes be brought to the house of the LORD (Num 13:20 in context of firstfruits; Exo 23:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines firstfruits as the fruit or produce first matured and collected in any season; and firstripe as first ripe, earliest matured.
webster_full: FIRST-FRUITS, n. The fruit or produce first matured and collected in any season.
2. The first profits of any thing.
FIRSTLING, n. The first produce or offspring; applied to beasts.
scriptures: Mic 7:1
Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits, as the grapegleanings of the vintage: there is no cluster to eat: my soul desired the firstripe fruit.
Hos 9:10

I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers as the firstripe in the fig tree at her first time: but they went to Baalpeor, and separated themselves unto that shame; and their abominations were according as they loved.
The first of the firstfruits of thy land thou shalt bring into the house of the LORD thy God. Thou shalt not seethe a kid in his mother's milk.
Isa 28:4

And the glorious beauty, which is on the head of the fat valley, shall be a fading flower, and as the hasty fruit before the summer; which when he that looketh upon it seeth, while it is yet in his hand he eateth it up.
corruption_summary: God is imagined as receiving worship dutifully, and Hosea describes His first sight of Israel as a man finding the first ripe fig of the season.
corruption_paragraphs: Hosea 9:10 records delight rather than obligation: I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers as the firstripe in the fig tree at her first time. The firstripe fig was eaten on the spot, prized because it was early and scarce. That is God describing His own pleasure in a people, and the verse's second half makes the fall from it worse: but they went to Baalpeor, and separated themselves unto that shame.

Micah 7:1 uses the same image for spiritual famine. Woe is me! for I am as when they have gathered the summer fruits… there is none upright among men. The prophet is walking through his own nation like a man in a stripped orchard, looking for one early fig and finding nothing. It is one of the loneliest verses in the prophets, and the book still ends with who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity.
roots_summary: Hebrew bikkurah (H1063), the first ripe fig; related to bikkurim, firstfruits — the offering brought to the sanctuary.
roots_lines: Hebrew bikkurah (H1063) — firstripe fig; Micah 7:1, Hosea 9:10, Isaiah 28:4.
Hebrew bikkurim (H1061) — firstfruits; Exodus 23:19, Leviticus 23:20.
Hebrew reshith (H7225) — beginning, firstfruits; Proverbs 3:9, honour the LORD with the firstfruits.
usage: “My soul desired the firstripe fruit” — a prophet in a stripped orchard.
“I saw your fathers as the firstripe in the fig tree” — God describing His own delight.
“The first of the firstfruits… thou shalt bring” — the earliest given away.

pos: adv. (with eager craving; rendering Hebrew batsa, Greek ekchuno)
etymology: From greedy, Old English graedig. The adverb marks the manner of pursuit, which Scripture treats as damning independent of the object.
biblical_def: Greedily describes eager craving. Proverbs says of the wicked, “he coveteth greedily all the day long” (Pro 21:26), setting it against the righteous who giveth and spareth not. Jude condemns those who “ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward” (Jud 11). Ezekiel indicts princes who “have greedily gained of thy neighbours by extortion” (Eze 22:12), and Isaiah calls the watchmen greedy dogs which can never have enough (Isa 56:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines greedily as with a keen appetite for food or drink; voraciously; ravenously; and with keen or ardent desire.
webster_full: GREEDILY, adv. With a keen appetite for food or drink; voraciously; ravenously.
2. With keen or ardent desire.
scriptures: He coveteth greedily all the day long: but the righteous giveth and spareth not.
Jud 11
Woe unto them! for they have gone in the way of Cain, and ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the gainsaying of Core.
In thee have they taken gifts to shed blood; thou hast taken usury and increase, and thou hast greedily gained of thy neighbours by extortion, and hast forgotten me, saith the Lord GOD.
Yea, they are greedy dogs which can never have enough, and they are shepherds that cannot understand: they all look to their own way, every one for his gain, from his quarter.
corruption_summary: Ambition inside ministry is excused by its object, and Jude's charge against Balaam's imitators is entirely about the manner — they ran greedily, for reward.
corruption_paragraphs: Jude 11 names three failures and gives each a verb of motion: they have gone in the way of Cain, and ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward, and perished in the gainsaying of Core. The Balaam clause is the one that lands on religious professionals. Balaam did not curse Israel; he could not. What he did was keep returning to the question because the fee was substantial, and Jude describes the imitators as running.

Isaiah 56:11 is the same charge aimed at shepherds: yea, they are greedy dogs which can never have enough, and they are shepherds that cannot understand: they all look to their own way, every one for his gain, from his quarter. The phrase can never have enough is the definition. Greed is not measured by what a man has taken but by the fact that no amount closes the account.
roots_summary: Hebrew batsa (H1214), to gain by violence, to be greedy of gain; nephesh azzah, a strong appetite; Greek ekchuno (G1632), to pour out, run riotously.
roots_lines: Hebrew batsa (H1214) — to gain unjustly, be greedy; Ezekiel 22:12, 27, Proverbs 1:19.
Hebrew avah (H183) — to desire greatly; Proverbs 21:26, he coveteth greedily all the day long.
Greek ekchuno (G1632) — to pour out, rush; Jude 11, ran greedily after the error of Balaam.
usage: “He coveteth greedily all the day long” — a settled occupation.
“Ran greedily after the error of Balaam for reward” — the manner is the charge.
“Greedy dogs which can never have enough” — the definition, applied to shepherds.

pos: adj. (different in kind; rendering Hebrew shanah, Aramaic shena)
etymology: From Latin diversus, turned different ways. In the law diverse marks forbidden mixtures; in Daniel it marks a beast unlike the others.
biblical_def: Diverse means different in kind. The law forbids diverse weights and measures: “Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small… for all that do such things… are an abomination unto the LORD thy God” (Deu 25:13,16). Daniel's fourth beast is “diverse from all the beasts that were before it” (Dan 7:7), and its little horn is “diverse from the first” (Dan 7:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines diverse as different; unlike; dissimilar; and in different directions, various.
webster_full: DIVERSE, a. Different; unlike; dissimilar.
2. In different directions; to different points.
3. Various; multiform.
scriptures: Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small.
For all that do such things, and all that do unrighteously, are an abomination unto the LORD thy God.
Dan 7:7

After this I saw in the night visions, and behold a fourth beast, dreadful and terrible, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth: it devoured and brake in pieces, and stamped the residue with the feet of it: and it was diverse from all the beasts that were before it; and it had ten horns.
Divers weights, and divers measures, both of them are alike abomination to the LORD.
corruption_summary: Two sets of standards are maintained for different people, and Deuteronomy calls a bag with a heavy stone and a light one an abomination.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 25:13-16 legislates against a very specific fraud: a merchant carrying two weights, a great and a small — the heavy one for buying, the light one for selling. Nothing is stolen visibly; every transaction looks fair. God's verdict on the practice uses the strongest word in the law: all that do such things, and all that do unrighteously, are an abomination unto the LORD thy God. Proverbs repeats it twice for emphasis.

The principle reaches well past commerce. Any person who applies one standard to himself and another to his neighbour, or one to allies and another to opponents, is carrying divers weights in his bag. The fraud is invisible in any single case and total across a lifetime, which is precisely why the law addresses the equipment rather than the individual transaction.
roots_summary: Hebrew shanah (H8138), to change or differ; Aramaic shena (H8133), diverse; the phrase eben va-eben, a stone and a stone, is the idiom for divers weights.
roots_lines: Hebrew eben va-eben — a stone and a stone; Deuteronomy 25:13, the literal idiom for divers weights.
Aramaic shena (H8133) — to be diverse, changed; Daniel 7:7, 19, 23-24.
Hebrew toebah (H8441) — abomination; Deuteronomy 25:16, Proverbs 20:10, 23.
usage: “Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights” — the equipment, not the transaction.
“Are an abomination unto the LORD thy God” — the law's strongest word.
“Diverse from all the beasts that were before it” — Daniel's fourth kingdom.

pos: adv. (with wisdom; rendering Hebrew sakal, Greek phronimos)
etymology: From wise. The adverb concerns conduct rather than knowledge — how a thing is done, not what is known.
biblical_def: Wisely means with practical wisdom. David “behaved himself wisely in all his ways; and the LORD was with him” — and Saul, seeing it, was afraid of him (1Sa 18:14–15). The psalmist resolves, “I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way… I will walk within my house with a perfect heart” (Psa 101:2). Christ commends an unjust steward “because he had done wisely” (Luk 16:8), and Pharaoh says of Israel, “let us deal wisely with them” (Exo 1:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines wisely as in a wise manner; prudently; judiciously; discreetly; with wisdom.
webster_full: WISELY, adv. In a wise manner; prudently; judiciously; discreetly; with wisdom.
2. Craftily; with art or stratagem.
scriptures: And David behaved himself wisely in all his ways; and the LORD was with him.
I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way. O when wilt thou come unto me? I will walk within my house with a perfect heart.
Luk 16:8
And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely: for the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light.
Exo 1:10

Come on, let us deal wisely with them; lest they multiply, and it come to pass, that, when there falleth out any war, they join also unto our enemies, and fight against us, and so get them up out of the land.
corruption_summary: Wisdom is treated as a quality of speech, and Scripture measures it by behaviour — David behaved himself wisely, and it made his enemy afraid.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Samuel 18:14-15 records a causal chain worth noticing: David behaved himself wisely in all his ways; and the LORD was with him. Wherefore when Saul saw that he behaved himself very wisely, he was afraid of him. Consistent wise conduct did not disarm Saul's hostility; it intensified it. Doing well is not a strategy for being left alone, and Scripture never suggests otherwise.

Psalm 101:2 adds the harder half: I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way. O when wilt thou come unto me? I will walk within my house with a perfect heart. The test of wise behaviour is located inside the house, where there is no audience and no advantage in it. A man may behave wisely in public for reasons that have nothing to do with wisdom; the domestic clause removes those reasons.
roots_summary: Hebrew sakal (H7919), to be prudent, act wisely, prosper; Greek phronimos (G5430), prudently — the adverb in Luke 16:8.
roots_lines: Hebrew sakal (H7919) — to act wisely, prosper; 1 Samuel 18:14-15, 30, Psalm 101:2.
Greek phronimos (G5430) — prudently, wisely; only Luke 16:8.
Hebrew chakam (H2449) — to be wise; the broader wisdom vocabulary.
usage: “He behaved himself wisely… and the LORD was with him” — and Saul grew afraid.
“I will walk within my house with a perfect heart” — the test with no audience.
“The lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely” — shrewdness noted, not the fraud.

pos: adj. (one's own, fitting; rendering Greek asteios and idios)
etymology: From Latin proprius, one's own. In older English proper means belonging to oneself, and secondarily fitting or comely.
biblical_def: Proper means one's own, or fitting. Hebrews says Moses was hid three months by his parents “because they saw he was a proper child; and they were not afraid of the king's commandment” (Heb 11:23) — a comely child, and the sight of him produced defiance. Paul says every man hath “his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that” (1Co 7:7), and David gave of “mine own proper good” to the house of God (1Ch 29:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines proper as peculiar; naturally or essentially belonging to a person or thing; not common; and well formed, comely.
webster_full: PROPER, a. Peculiar; naturally or essentially belonging to a person or thing; not common.
2. Belonging to many or to all; not common.
3. One's own.
4. Fit; suitable; adapted; accommodated.
5. Well formed; handsome.
scriptures: By faith Moses, when he was born, was hid three months of his parents, because they saw he was a proper child; and they were not afraid of the king's commandment.
For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that.

Moreover, because I have set my affection to the house of my God, I have of mine own proper good, of gold and silver, which I have given to the house of my God, over and above all that I have prepared for the holy house,
Exo 2:2
And the woman conceived, and bare a son: and when she saw him that he was a goodly child, she hid him three months.
corruption_summary: Courage is expected to come from conviction alone, and Hebrews traces one famous act of defiance to parents looking at their child.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 11:23 makes an unusual causal claim: by faith Moses, when he was born, was hid three months of his parents, because they saw he was a proper child; and they were not afraid of the king's commandment. The faith is credited to Amram and Jochebed, and its trigger is what they saw when they looked at their son. Something about the child persuaded them that the state's decree could be defied. Faith here begins with attention rather than argument.

1 Corinthians 7:7 uses the other sense and settles a common anxiety: every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that. The context is marriage and singleness, and Paul refuses to rank them. Each is a gift, each is proper to the person who has it, and neither is a defective version of the other.
roots_summary: Greek asteios (G791), elegant, comely — used of Moses; idios (G2398), one's own; Hebrew segullah (H5459), a peculiar treasure.
roots_lines: Greek asteios (G791) — comely, proper; Hebrews 11:23, Acts 7:20, exceeding fair.
Greek idios (G2398) — one's own, proper; 1 Corinthians 7:7, Acts 1:19.
Hebrew segullah (H5459) — peculiar treasure, proper good; 1 Chronicles 29:3, Exodus 19:5.
usage: “They saw he was a proper child” — defiance that began with looking.
“Every man hath his proper gift of God” — neither state is defective.
“Mine own proper good” — David's personal treasure given to the house.

pos: adv., adj. (wrongly, out of order; rendering Aramaic shalu, Greek kakos)
etymology: From a- and miss. To do amiss is to miss the mark — the same figure as the main Greek word for sin.
biblical_def: Amiss means wrongly. James diagnoses unanswered prayer with it: “Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts” (Jas 4:3). The dying thief defends Christ: “this man hath done nothing amiss” (Luk 23:41). Daniel's accusers can find no error or fault in him, no thing amiss (Dan 6:4), and Solomon's dedication prayer anticipates the people confessing, “We have sinned, and have done perversely, we have committed wickedness” (2Ch 6:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines amiss as in a faulty manner; contrary to propriety, truth, law or morality; and improperly, unsuitably.
webster_full: AMISS, a. or adv. Wrong; faulty; out of order; improper; as, it may not be amiss to ask advice.
2. In a faulty manner; contrary to propriety, truth, law or morality.
3. Wrong; erroneous.
scriptures: Jas 4:3
Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.
And we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss.
Dan 6:4

Then the presidents and princes sought to find occasion against Daniel concerning the kingdom; but they could find none occasion nor fault; forasmuch as he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him.
Jas 4:2
Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not.
corruption_summary: Unanswered prayer is blamed on God's silence or the asker's weak faith, and James names a third possibility — the request itself was wrong.
corruption_paragraphs: James 4:2-3 walks through the options in order: ye have not, because ye ask not. Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts. The first failure is not asking; the second is asking with the intention of spending the answer on oneself. Neither is a mystery of providence. James treats prayer as a request with a stated purpose, and God as a Father who reads the purpose.

Luke 23:41 puts the word in the mouth of a criminal minutes from death, and it is one of the clearest verdicts on Christ in the Gospels: we indeed justly; for we receive the due reward of our deeds: but this man hath done nothing amiss. A dying thief made an accurate assessment of his own guilt and Christ's innocence in a single sentence, and then asked to be remembered.
roots_summary: Aramaic shalu (H7960), a fault or error; Greek atopos (G824), out of place, amiss; kakos (G2560), badly, wrongly.
roots_lines: Greek kakos (G2560) — badly, amiss; James 4:3, ye ask amiss.
Greek atopos (G824) — out of place, improper; Luke 23:41, this man hath done nothing amiss.
Aramaic shalu (H7960) — fault, error; Daniel 6:4, neither was there any error or fault found in him.
usage: “Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss” — the request itself examined.
“This man hath done nothing amiss” — a dying thief's accurate verdict.
“Neither was there any error or fault found in him” — Daniel audited by enemies.

pos: adj. (unceasing; rendering Hebrew tamid, Greek adialeiptos)
etymology: From Latin continuare, to join without break. The Hebrew tamid named the daily offering — the sacrifice that never lapsed.
biblical_def: Continual means unceasing. Scripture applies it to the burnt offering — “a continual burnt offering throughout your generations at the door of the tabernacle” (Exo 29:42) — and to a cheerful heart: “he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast” (Pro 15:15). Paul reports “great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart” for his kinsmen (Rom 9:2), and Christ commends the widow whose continual coming wearied an unjust judge (Luk 18:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines continual as proceeding without interruption or cessation; unceasing; and very frequent, often repeated.
webster_full: CONTINUAL, a. Proceeding without interruption or cessation; unceasing; not intermitting.
2. Very frequent; often repeated; as, he makes continual complaints.
scriptures: This shall be a continual burnt offering throughout your generations at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation before the LORD: where I will meet you, to speak there unto thee.
All the days of the afflicted are evil: but he that is of a merry heart hath a continual feast.
Rom 9:2
That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart.
Luk 18:5
Yet because this widow troubleth me, I will avenge her, lest by her continual coming she weary me.
corruption_summary: Persistence in prayer is mistaken for a lack of faith, and Christ's own parable makes an unjust judge yield to a widow's continual coming.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 18 is prefaced with its purpose stated outright: he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint. The widow's method is simply repetition — her continual coming — and the judge relents to be rid of her. Christ's argument is from the lesser to the greater: if an unjust judge yields to persistence, shall not God avenge his own elect, which cry day and night unto him? Persistence is not nagging heaven; it is the posture Christ prescribed.

Romans 9:2 shows that continual can name sorrow as easily as joy: I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart, for Paul's unbelieving countrymen. He says it immediately after Romans 8's triumph about nothing separating us from the love of God. Settled assurance and unbroken grief for others occupy the same heart in the same chapter, which is worth remembering before diagnosing sorrow as unbelief.
roots_summary: Hebrew tamid (H8548), continually, the daily offering; Greek adialeiptos (G88), unceasing; diapantos (G1275), always.
roots_lines: Hebrew tamid (H8548) — continual, daily; Exodus 29:42, Numbers 28:3-6.
Greek adialeiptos (G88) — unceasing; Romans 9:2, 2 Timothy 1:3.
Greek hupopiazo (G5299) — to wear out by continual coming; Luke 18:5.
usage: “A continual burnt offering throughout your generations” — the fire that never lapsed.
“Lest by her continual coming she weary me” — the widow's method.
“A merry heart hath a continual feast” — a table set by disposition.
